name: Thomson's cathode-ray tube (1897)
description: J. J. Thomson deflected cathode rays with charged plates and showed they are negative particles: electrons. Here an electron at 0.2 c must hit a one-cell spot on the screen. Two electron energies must hit their own one-cell spots: the deflection falls as 1/T, like in an oscilloscope. Build deflection plates from point charges.

reality.represents: Thomson's cathode-ray tube (1897): electrons deflected electrically

remarks.detail: Through a given field a faster particle spends less time and is kicked less: the spot of an oscilloscope moves in proportion to the deflecting voltage over the beam's energy.
Thomson deflected the rays between two parallel metal plates at a voltage, a nearly uniform field; here you build the field from point charges.

remarks.line: The magnetic half of the experiment
remarks.detail: Thomson balanced the electric deflection against a magnetic one to measure the electrons' charge-to-mass ratio; only the electric part is here.
Hertz had failed to see the electric deflection: ionized gas in his tube screened the plates. Thomson's better vacuum made it visible; here the vacuum is perfect.

Everything is symmetric about the plane z = 0, so the particle never leaves it. A real beam also has a width across the plane, where the same fields act differently (focusing in the plane can defocus across it).
